name: Trusted Execution Environments
description: TEEs and enclaves (Intel SGX, ARM TrustZone, TDX, SEV), attestation, and confidential computing.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list reflect a field reckoning with the fragility of hardware enclaves just as they reached mainstream processors. Foreshadow (USENIX 2018) was a watershed, showing that transient out-of-order execution could extract the very attestation keys underpinning Intel SGX, while The Guard's Dilemma (USENIX 2018) demonstrated practical code-reuse attacks against enclave code itself. Parallel work questioned other roots of trust, with A Bad Dream (USENIX 2018) subverting the Trusted Platform Module via power-management states. The early message was clear: the hardware promised isolation, but its microarchitectural and lifecycle assumptions leaked.

A second wave broadened the attack and defense surface beyond SGX. Researchers turned to ARM TrustZone, with PARTEMU (USENIX 2020) enabling dynamic analysis of real-world trusted OSes and Horizontal Privilege Escalation in Trusted Applications (USENIX 2020) exposing weak isolation between trusted apps. At the same time, tooling matured for finding enclave bugs systematically, from TeeRex (USENIX 2020) discovering memory-corruption in SGX enclaves to SGXFuzz (USENIX 2022) synthesizing nested input structures for fuzzing. A complementary thread treated the host-enclave boundary as adversarial in both directions, as in SGXLock and SGXLock's mutual-distrust model and A Hardware-Software Co-design for Efficient Intra-Enclave Isolation (both USENIX 2022). Builders also began delivering real confidential-computing systems, such as Visor (USENIX 2020) for private video analytics and Civet (USENIX 2020) for partitioning Java into enclaves.

The center of gravity then shifted toward confidential VMs and AMD SEV. CIPHERLEAKS (USENIX 2021) introduced the ciphertext side channel that broke constant-time crypto on SEV, and VoltPillager (USENIX 2021) revived hardware fault injection against SGX via voltage scaling. This line continued into recent attacks on VM-granularity TEEs, with HECKLER (USENIX 2024) weaponizing malicious interrupts and CacheWarp (USENIX 2024) using selective state reset as software fault injection. Defensively, the field moved from patching to principled assurance, including formally verified hypervisor memory protection (USENIX 2021), DICE* (USENIX 2021) for verified measured boot, and AEX-Notify (USENIX 2023), a co-designed mitigation for precise single-stepping adopted into Intel SGX.

Today the area spans new hardware abstractions and richer use cases. SHELTER (USENIX 2023) extends Arm CCA with user-space isolation, ReZone (USENIX 2022) reduces TrustZone TEE privilege, and attestation work scales to fleets and real-time systems, as in SCRAPS (USENIX 2022) for pub-sub IoT and ARI (USENIX 2023) for mission-execution integrity. Confidential computing has also become a deployment substrate, with Reusable Enclaves (USENIX 2023) targeting serverless workloads. The arc runs from demonstrating that enclaves leak, to building tools and systems around them, to defending VM-scale TEEs with formal methods and hardware-software co-design.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection treated the Intel SGX enclave as a promising but leaky box. Even with memory encrypted, an attacker watching the pattern of accesses could learn secrets, so "ZeroTrace : Oblivious Memory Primitives from Intel SGX" (NDSS 2018) and "OBLIVIATE: A Data Oblivious Filesystem for Intel SGX" (NDSS 2018) layered oblivious-RAM techniques over SGX to hide access patterns. This obliviousness theme proved durable, resurfacing in "OblivSketch: Oblivious Network Measurement as a Cloud Service" and "DOVE: A Data-Oblivious Virtual Environment" (both NDSS 2021).

The field then broadened along two axes. First, TEEs escaped Intel's monopoly: "SANCTUARY: ARMing TrustZone with User-space Enclaves" (NDSS 2019) carved user-space enclaves out of ARM TrustZone, while "TIMBER-V: Tag-Isolated Memory Bringing Fine-grained Enclaves to RISC-V" (NDSS 2019) brought enclaves to open hardware. Second, researchers hardened the trust boundary itself: "Emilia: Catching Iago in Legacy Code" (NDSS 2021) systematized the danger of a malicious OS feeding enclaves poisoned syscall results, and "CHANCEL: Efficient Multi-client Isolation Under Adversarial Programs" (NDSS 2021) tackled isolating mutually distrusting clients. Alongside, TEEs became a building block for larger systems in "Custos: Practical Tamper-Evident Auditing of Operating Systems Using Trusted Execution" (NDSS 2020) and "Hybrid Trust Multi-party Computation with Trusted Execution Environment" (NDSS 2022).

By the mid-2020s the frontier moved to confidential computing at scale. "CAGE: Complementing Arm CCA with GPU Extensions" (NDSS 2024) and "RContainer" (NDSS 2025) built on ARM's new CCA architecture, extending protection to accelerators and containers, while attacks kept pace: "Faults in Our Bus: Novel Bus Fault Attack to Break ARM TrustZone" (NDSS 2024) and "CounterSEVeillance: Performance-Counter Attacks on AMD SEV-SNP" (NDSS 2025) showed that whole-VM protections like AMD SEV-SNP inherit their own side channels. "The Road to Trust: Building Enclaves within Confidential VMs" (NDSS 2025) tried to reconcile the fine-grained enclave model with the coarse confidential-VM model, and tooling matured through "EnclaveFuzz: Finding Vulnerabilities in SGX Applications" (NDSS 2024).

The most recent work shows a field simultaneously automating its own construction and absorbing relentless attack pressure. "Automated Code Annotation with LLMs for Establishing TEE Boundaries" (NDSS 2026) turns large language models loose on the hard problem of partitioning code across the trust line, and "SoK: Analysis of Accelerator TEE Designs" (NDSS 2026) steps back to systematize the crowded accelerator-TEE space. Meanwhile attackers refuse to relent: "DNN Latency Sequencing: Extracting DNN Architectures from Intel SGX Enclaves with Single-Stepping Attacks" and "SNPeek: Side-Channel Analysis for Privacy Applications on Confidential VMs" (both NDSS 2026) extract secrets from the very enclaves and confidential VMs the field has spent years fortifying, and "Breaking Isolation: A New Perspective on Hypervisor Exploitation via Cross-Domain Attacks" (NDSS 2026) probes the isolation boundary from a fresh angle. Trusted execution has grown from a single leaky SGX box into a sprawling ecosystem of architectures, but the cat-and-mouse contest between isolation and side channels remains its defining rhythm.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection treats trusted execution as a building block to be put to use, then immediately stress-tested. EnclaveDB: A Secure Database Using SGX (S&P 2018) showed that Intel SGX could shelter a real system — a database engine with confidentiality, integrity, and freshness guarantees — while Racing in Hyperspace (S&P 2018) already flagged that hyper-threading side channels could leak from those same enclaves. From the start, the story is a race between what enclaves promise and what the underlying silicon quietly reveals.

That tension exploded in 2019-2020 as microarchitectural attacks matured. RIDL: Rogue In-Flight Data Load (S&P 2019) siphoned in-flight data out of SGX through transient execution, and LVI: Hijacking Transient Execution (S&P 2020) inverted the idea to inject attacker data into a victim. Plundervolt (S&P 2020) and later PLATYPUS (S&P 2021) weaponized power and voltage interfaces, blurring the line between software and physical attacks. Meanwhile the field widened beyond Intel: SoK: Understanding the Prevailing Security Vulnerabilities in TrustZone-assisted TEE Systems (S&P 2020) catalogued ARM TrustZone's weaknesses, and SEVurity (S&P 2020) broke AMD SEV's integrity-free memory encryption — the first cracks in the confidential-VM model.

The 2021-2023 window mixed hardening with new applications. A Secure and Formally Verified Linux KVM Hypervisor (S&P 2021) brought proof-based assurance to the virtualization layer, while A Systematic Look at Ciphertext Side Channels on AMD SEV-SNP (S&P 2022) exposed a leak that would haunt confidential VMs for years. Researchers also turned enclaves toward machine learning and better tooling — ShadowNet (S&P 2023) for on-device inference, and TEEzz (S&P 2023) plus later SyzTrust (S&P 2024) fuzzing trusted apps and trusted OSes to find bugs at scale.

The most recent work converges on two themes: TEE-shielded ML is not as private as hoped, and physical attacks have become cheap. No Privacy Left Outside (S&P 2024) and CipherSteal (S&P 2025) reconstruct model inputs from TEE-protected neural networks, the latter riding exactly the ciphertext side channels flagged in 2022, while SoK: SGX.Fail (S&P 2024) tallies a decade of exposures. The frontier, though, is hardware interposition: BadRAM (S&P 2025) demonstrated practical memory-aliasing attacks, and 2026 brings a wave of them — TEE.Fail: Breaking Trusted Execution Environments via DDR5 Memory Bus Interposition, Battering RAM's low-cost interposer, BreakFAST against AMD's Infinity Fabric, and VMSCAPE and TDXRay probing branch-predictor and side-channel gaps in Intel TDX and cloud VMs. After eight years, the guarantees have moved from "isolated from all software" to a hard-won admission that an attacker with a cheap interposer on the memory bus can still get in.

ccs.narrative:
TEE security at CCS has examined Intel SGX, ARM TrustZone, and AMD SEV from both attack and defense perspectives. Nemesis: Studying Microarchitectural Timing Leaks in Rudimentary CPU Interrupt Logic (CCS 2018) revealed that the timing of SGX enclave interrupts leaks secret-dependent behavior. A Tale of Two Worlds: Assessing the Vulnerability of Enclave Shielding Runtimes (CCS 2019) systematically assessed the trusted-untrusted interface in enclave shielding runtimes, finding widespread exploitable bugs across multiple SDKs.

TrustZone attacks expanded in 2019: VoltJockey: Breaching TrustZone by Software-Controlled Voltage Manipulation over Multi-core Frequencies (CCS 2019) induced faults in the secure world via voltage underscaling, Hardware-Backed Heist: Extracting ECDSA Keys from Qualcomm's TrustZone (CCS 2019) extracted private keys via microarchitectural side channels, and SecTEE: A Software-based Approach to Secure Enclave Architecture Using TEE (CCS 2019) built a software-only enclave system on top of TrustZone. LightBox: Full-stack Protected Stateful Middlebox at Lightning Speed (CCS 2019) ran stateful network middleboxes inside SGX at line speed.

Fault injection continued to evolve: One Glitch to Rule Them All: Fault Injection Attacks Against AMD's Secure Encrypted Virtualization (CCS 2021) mounted voltage glitching against AMD SEV's secure processor, breaking VM memory encryption. SmashEx: Smashing SGX Enclaves Using Exceptions (CCS 2021) exploited exception-handling re-entrancy to corrupt enclave state.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list arrives at a moment of both optimism and alarm about Intel SGX. On the defensive side, researchers were busy showing what enclaves could build: secure databases in EnclaveDB (S&P 2018), oblivious memory and filesystems in ZeroTrace (NDSS 2018) and OBLIVIATE (NDSS 2018) to hide access patterns from a hostile OS. But the same year, Foreshadow: Extracting the Keys to the Intel SGX Kingdom (USENIX 2018) used transient out-of-order execution to lift SGX's sealing and attestation keys outright, and Nemesis (CCS 2018) and The Guard's Dilemma (USENIX 2018) showed that interrupt timing and code-reuse gave attackers even more leverage inside the enclave. The founding tension of the field was set: TEEs were being pitched as a trust anchor at the very moment their microarchitectural foundations were proving leaky.

Through 2019 and 2020 the attack surface widened on two axes. First, ARM TrustZone got serious scrutiny alongside SGX — SANCTUARY (NDSS 2019) added user-space enclaves, TIMBER-V (NDSS 2019) brought enclaves to RISC-V, while Hardware-Backed Heist (CCS 2019) extracted ECDSA keys from Qualcomm's TrustZone and the SoK on TrustZone-assisted TEEs (S&P 2020) tied the whole messy landscape together. Second, researchers moved from passive leakage to active fault injection: VoltJockey (CCS 2019), Plundervolt (S&P 2020), and later VoltPillager (USENIX 2021) weaponized voltage and frequency scaling, while LVI (S&P 2020) inverted Spectre-style injection into the enclave. Crucially, A Tale of Two Worlds (CCS 2019) and TeeRex (USENIX 2020) pointed out that the boring glue code at the trusted/untrusted boundary was itself a rich vulnerability class, independent of any silicon flaw.

The 2021–2022 window is dominated by AMD SEV and the discovery that encrypting VM memory is not enough. SEVurity (S&P 2020) had already broken integrity-free memory encryption; CIPHERLEAKS (USENIX 2021) then named the ciphertext side channel, and CrossLine (CCS 2021) plus One Glitch to Rule Them All (CCS 2021) broke SEV's isolation and injected faults. The sobering punchline came with A Systematic Look at Ciphertext Side Channels on AMD SEV-SNP (S&P 2022): the very SEV generation meant to close these holes still leaked. Alongside, PLATYPUS (S&P 2021) and AEPIC Leak (USENIX 2022) added power and architectural-register leakage, and the community began investing in verified foundations, as in the formally verified KVM hypervisor (S&P 2021).

The most recent work, clustered in 2026, shows a field that has matured in both its threats and its ambitions. Attacks now target what runs inside enclaves rather than just the enclave itself: DNN Latency Sequencing (NDSS 2026) reconstructs neural-network architectures from SGX via single-stepping, and SNPeek (NDSS 2026) carries the ciphertext side channel forward onto confidential VMs. Physical attacks have not gone away — TEE.Fail (S&P 2026) breaks modern TEEs by interposing on the DDR5 memory bus. At the same time the defensive agenda has broadened toward practical deployment concerns: rollback and state-freshness in Pallas and Aegis (NDSS 2026) and secure auditable state rollback for confidential cloud apps (S&P 2026), stronger attestation in EXIA (NDSS 2026), and forward-looking systematization in the SoK on Accelerator TEE Designs (NDSS 2026). Tellingly, Automated Code Annotation with LLMs for Establishing TEE Boundaries (NDSS 2026) folds large language models into the tooling — a sign the field is now as much about making confidential computing usable and correct at scale as it is about the next microarchitectural break.
